content:
In Italy, finishing dinner doesn’t necessarily mean the evening is over. In fact, a key part of the Italian dinner experience comes after all the food is gone. While the country’s aperitivo culture is all about easing into a meal, digestivo is about what follows it.

The tradition comes from the centuries-old practice of infusing alcohol with herbs, roots, and other botanicals for their medicinal and digestive benefits. While some popular digestivi are still consumed for their perceived digestive advantages, the practice has shifted over time from one of function to enjoyment. The digestivo has become an important part of Italian dining culture.

Typically served neat in small glasses, the digestivi range from intensely herbal amari to sweet citrus liqueurs and powerful grape-based spirits. And just as Italy’s regional cuisines vary dramatically from north to south, so do these liqueurs. From those of northern Italy to the sunny Amalfi Coast, each offers a different glimpse into the country’s drinking history.

Grappa: Northern Italy’s Grape-Based Spirit

Grappa is a spirit made from grape pomace, which are the skins, seeds, and other solids left behind after grapes are pressed for winemaking.

The practice of distilling the leftovers developed over centuries, particularly in northern Italy, where regions such as Veneto, Trentino-Alto Adige, and Piemonte became important centers of grappa production. 

While grappa production began in rural communities that wanted to use every part of the grape harvest, grappa gradually evolved from a rustic spirit into a sophisticated category of its own.

Today, producers make everything from clear, unaged grappa to expressions aged in wooden barrels. Depending on the grapes and production method, grappa characteristics can range from floral and fruity to rich and spicy.

Grappa is traditionally served neat after dinner, but is also sometimes added to espresso in a preparation known as caffè corretto, or “corrected coffee.”

Amari: Diverse and Cocktail-Ready 

Italian amari are served after meals and span flavor profiles. It is made by infusing a base alcohol with a mix of bittering agents, herbs, roots, flowers, and citrus peels, then sweetening and aging the liquid.

Amaro leggero (light) has lower bitterness, is floral and citrusy, rounds out with a gentle sweetness, and is viewed as a gateway to darker amari. Amaro medio (medium) has a balanced bittersweetness and the flavor profile can include cola, caramel, licorice and citrus peel. Rabarbaro, or rhubarb root, has a smoky, earthy, slightly medicinal character. Alpine or mountain amaro is often drier and resinous, driven by mountain hers and pines.

While amaro is typically sipped neat as a digestivo, it’s also a favorite ingredient in various modern cocktails. Some of these include: the Black Manhattan: a sophisticated nightcap that swaps out traditional sweet vermouth for a rich, dark amaro, alongside rye whiskey and bitters, the Toronto: a classic whiskey riff combining rye whiskey, fernet, simple syrup and bitters.

Sambuca: Central Italy’s Anise-Flavored Traditional Beverage

For many drinkers, sambuca’s distinctive licorice-like flavor is instantly identifiable. The sweet, anise-flavored liqueur has particularly strong ties to Civitavecchia, a port city in Lazio, where commercial sambuca production developed during the 19th century. 

Most sambuca is consumed neat after dinner. However, it’s also commonly served con la mosca, or “with the fly,” a preparation featuring three coffee beans floating in the glass. The beans add aroma and a visual flourish, with the representation of the number three historically associated with health, happiness, and prosperity.

Another favorite Italian ritual that deserves its place on any table around the world is to add a little sambuca to espresso as to enhance after-dinner coffee.

Limoncello: Southern Italy’s Sunshine in a Glass

Limoncello is arguably one of Italy’s most famous after-dinner drinks, and unlike most herbal digestivi, limoncello doesn’t contain bitter roots or complex spice blends, making it one of the sweeter after-dinner options. 

Like many cocktails and spirits, its precise origins are debated, with several communities claiming a role in its creation. 

But the spirit is most closely associated with southern Italy, particularly the Sorrento Peninsula, Amalfi Coast, and the island of Capri, and celebrates one of the region’s most recognizable agricultural products: lemons.

Limoncello is traditionally made by steeping lemon peels in alcohol, then combining the infusion with sugar and water. The process extracts the aromatic oils from the peel, creating a fragrant, intensely citrusy sweet liqueur that can be enjoyed neat, in a spritz variation, and a host of other cocktails, especially those in the low ABV category.

A Tradition Worth Savoring

The range of Italian digestivi tells a story of regional ingredients, resourcefulness, and centuries of drinking traditions.

While these liqueurs were historically associated with aiding digestion, their appeal today has much more to do with flavor preference, hospitality, and the pleasure of extending a meal just a little longer.

They are a great incentive to not rush away from the dinner table.

title: The Surprising History Behind Italy’s Most Beloved Pre-dinner Drinks
summary:
In Italy, drinking before dinner isn’t just a way to start the evening. It’s a tradition. The aperitivo, or pre-dinner drink, is a custom that has been deeply rooted in Italian culture for generations. The idea behind the practice, much like America’s happy hour, is to ease into the evening starting with a few snacks and a drink to awaken the palate.  Today, the aperitivo is mostly associated with a chic cocktail sipped at a table in a bustling piazza. However, Aperitivo is no new trend. It is a rich, storied Italian tradition that many Americans are only now discovering.

content:
In Italy, drinking before dinner isn’t just a way to start the evening. It’s a tradition.

The aperitivo, or pre-dinner drink, is a custom that has been deeply rooted in Italian culture for generations. The idea behind the practice, much like America’s happy hour, is to ease into the evening starting with a few snacks and a drink to awaken the palate. 

Today, the aperitivo is mostly associated with a chic cocktail sipped at a table in a bustling piazza. However, Aperitivo is no new trend. It is a rich, storied Italian tradition that many Americans are only now discovering.

For centuries Italians have been drinking aperitivi, fortified wines infused with herbs as well as botanical liqueurs, which were thought to have medicinal properties. Today this category includes some of Italy’s most iconic spirits, each one bringing a bit of its local tradition to the glass. 

Vermouth: The Turin Original

Vermouth is a core component of Italy’s aperitivo culture, not only as an elegant pour on its own but also as one of the quintessential cocktail modifiers. The vermouth we drink today originated in Turin, the capital of the Piemonte region in northern Italy.

In 1786, the first sweet red vermouth was created by mixing wine with sugar and adding its own blend of herbs and spices. Today’s versions resemble the original recipe, with fortified wine as a base that is then aromatized with a special combination of herbs, roots, and spices.

Today, sweet red vermouth continues its popularity, traditionally served neat or on the rocks with a slice of citrus. Vermouth is also an essential ingredient in some of the most famous cocktails in the world such as the Negroni, Manhattan, and the Americano.

Red Bitters: The Rise of Bittersweet Aperitivo

In the 1860s, red bitter liqueurs were introduced, which really cemented the tradition of bittersweet pre-dinner drinks. The bitter botanicals like gentian root, wormwood, cinchona bark, and bitter orange peel found in red bitter liqueur activate bitter taste receptors on the tongue. This immediately signals the salivary glands to produce more saliva, which moistens the mouth and prepares your taste buds to perceive food flavors more vividly.

Red bitter liqueurs are about 20–28% ABV, higher proof and more assertive, and act as the backbone of drinks like the Negroni and Americano, and of course, various spritzes.

Carciofo: The Unexpected Artichoke Aperitivo

Some of Italy’s most interesting liqueurs are made with ingredients you might never expect to find in a cocktail. Artichokes, for instance, are the star ingredient in a category of bittersweet herbal liqueurs known as carciofo.

While an artichoke-based liqueur might sound unusual, the vegetable has a long history in Italian food culture, particularly in regions where artichokes are widely cultivated.

Despite their unusual main ingredient, these liqueurs don’t necessarily taste like artichokes. Instead, artichoke leaves are combined with herbs, roots, and other botanicals to create complex flavors that tend to be earthy, herbal, and pleasantly bitter, often balanced by a touch of sweetness.

Artichoke-based amari gained wider popularity during the 20th century, particularly as Italy’s postwar café culture flourished. By the 1960s and 1970s, they had become a familiar part of the country’s aperitivo tradition, enjoyed as a way to unwind before dinner.

Today, carciofo liqueurs are commonly served over ice or topped with soda water for a simple aperitivo. Their distinctive bittersweet flavor also makes them a versatile cocktail ingredient. They can be used in a Negroni variation in place of the traditional red bitter aperitivo, adding a deeper, earthier character to the drink. They’re also well suited to a Spritz, mixed with prosecco and soda water, or a Little Italy, a Manhattan-inspired cocktail that combines rye whiskey, sweet vermouth, and artichoke amaro.

Rosolio: A Historic Liqueur Returns

Long before red bitter spritzes became so popular, another Italian liqueur was offered to guests at parties and gatherings: rosolio.

Rosolio is on the sweeter and more delicate flavor spectrum of aperitivi. Locally, it’s a classic pour for guests at special occasions and family gatherings.

Made from a recipe that includes flowers, herbs, fruits and spices grown nearby, this traditional drink was, until recently, produced almost exclusively by families in the central and southern regions of Italy. It’s traditionally served with sparkling wine or tonic, though it has now found its way onto the menus of some of the most influential cocktail bars around the world.

An Italian Tradition That Continues to Evolve

From the historic vermouth houses of Piemonte to the bergamot groves of Calabria, Italy’s aperitivo culture is as varied as the regions that helped shape it.

Each category brings something different to the table. Vermouth adds herbal complexity to classic cocktails, while bitter liqueurs offer bartenders a way to balance sweetness and introduce new layers of flavor. Meanwhile, floral, citrus-forward rosolio brings a lighter touch to spritzes and other refreshing drinks.

While these spirits have deep roots in Italian tradition, their influence now extends well beyond Italy. Bartenders around the world are finding new ways to incorporate them into both classic and contemporary cocktails, introducing a new generation of drinkers to ingredients that have been enjoyed in Italy for centuries.

The core of aperitivo culture remains the same as when it began. At its heart, enjoying aperitivi is still about taking a little time before dinner to relax, share a drink, and perhaps catch up with friends and family.

content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Stoli’s return to the U.S., Modelo’s deal with the NCAA, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Stoli makes U.S. comeback 11 months after liquidation filing: Stoli Group USA — the American arm of the Luxembourg-based wine and spirits company — announced its return to U.S. markets after a series of bankruptcy filings. The return will bring Stoli Vodka back to American shelves, as well as an expanded portfolio that includes Moskovskaya vodka, Rooster Rojo and KAH tequilas, and The Irishman and Writers’ Tears Irish whiskeys. Stoli Group USA first filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in November 2024, owing $84 million in debt at the time, before a judge converted it to a Chapter 7 liquidation in January of this year. After reaching a settlement with creditors, Stoli can now resume business in the U.S.
  • Modelo named first official beer of NCAA: Constellation Brands inked a deal with the National Collegiate Athletics Association (NCAA) naming Modelo the first official beer of the association. The partnership will center around March Madness — the association’s marquee tournament — as well as the College World Series, Frozen Four, and other major championships. The collaboration also offers Constellation exclusive ready-to-drink sponsorship rights, which the company will use to boost the presence of the recently acquired SpikedAde. Constellation’s deal with the NCAA is the latest example of the alcohol industry’s broader push to expand its footprint in the sports space.
  • Alabama restaurants, hotels missing popular booze brands after ABC mishap: Supply shortages in Alabama’s Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) warehouses are leaving restaurants and hotels in the state without beloved brands like Tito’s, Jack Daniel’s, and Jameson. Many operators have reported multiple weeks of missing or incomplete orders and significant losses in sales as a result. The shortages came after the state’s ABC moved to a new distribution warehouse and caused significant delays in order fulfillments. Mississippi, also a control state, endured a nearly identical fiasco earlier this year.

Product releases to watch:

  • LALO unveils 2026 High Proof bottling: The popular Austin-based tequila brand released the latest addition to its annual High Proof series. Bottled at 48 percent ABV, LALO’s 2026 High Proof is now available across 41 states for a suggested retail price of $74.99.
  • Atheras Spirits forays into gin and vodka: Atheras Spirits, a Brooklyn-based small-batch distillery that launched in 2024 with amari and liqueurs, expanded its portfolio with two gins and a vodka. Gin East ($41), Gin West ($37), and Monks Vodka ($33) will be available in New York and New Jersey later this year followed by a larger distribution to Connecticut; Washington, D.C.; Maryland; and Illinois in 2027.
  • Cazcanes celebrates its 10th anniversary with high-proof extra añejo: Cazcanes Tequila released Extra Añejo No. 10 Tributo Edition to honor the brand’s first decade of distilling. The extra añejo was bottled at 54 percent ABV, 14 percent higher than the required minimum. Just 3,650 bottles of Extra Añejo No. 10 Tributo Edition are available online for $499.99.
  • Buzzard’s Roost drops newest Cigar Rye bottling: The Louisville, Ky.-based brand released the third edition of its Cigar Rye series, following up on its fan-favorite collection. Buzzard’s Roost Cigar Rye #3 is now available onsite, online, and at retailers nationwide for a suggested retail price of $84.99.

content:
When you move into a new house in the Phillipines, salt is a common housewarming gift. “Filipinos are a very superstitious group of people,” Darwin Pornel, the co-owner of New York City’s new Filipino-American cocktail bar June Baby, says. “It’s for good luck and prosperity in your new home.”

So when Pornel, Roxanne Diaz Bangalan, and Ben Rojo were ready to swing open the doors of their East Village bar last month, it was a welcome gesture when they received a giant sphere of salt as a congratulatory gift. The rare Filipino sea salt, called Asín tibuók, was a gift from Mary Palac, the Mexican spirits portfolio ambassador for Campari America, whom Pornel calls an “ate,” meaning big sister.

Produced on Bohol Island in the Philippines, Asín tibuók is a large piece of unbroken sea salt that’s made through a traditional method passed down since at least the 1600s. To make the salt, craftspeople collect coconut husks and soak them in seawater for months. The husks are then dried and slowly burned over about a week and mixed with seawater to create a brine. The brine is boiled in clay pots, eventually forming a mound of smoky sea salt that resembles a white, cracked dinosaur egg in a brown shell. The four-month production process is so painstaking that it’s been named to the UNESCO list of intangible cultural heritage in need of urgent safeguarding and is becoming difficult to find even in Bohol.

In the Philippines, it’s often used as finishing salt dusted over fresh-caught fish or savory rice porridge. But at June Baby, the salt is shaved over an Old Fashioned riff called Taste and See. Bourbon fat washed with brown butter, rich date syrup, and a splash of Madeira come together for a cozy, warming cocktail. The drink’s flavor profile takes inspiration from a dessert that Pornel ate every Christmas called Food of the Gods, a blondie-style bar made with brown sugar, dates, and walnut

At June Baby, when a guest orders the Taste and See, the bartender finishes the build with a theatrical finishing touch, pulling out the large hunk of salt to grate over the drink with a microplane. Pornel says it’s an “absolute showstopper.”

But the salt is much more than just an eye-catching garnish, it’s an “if you know, you know” nod to the community that the team is catering to at June Baby. “We intentionally designed the space without very common motifs of Filipino culture like the flag or the sun and stars,” he says. “It’s such a payoff when people see the salt, they’re like, ‘oh my god, you guys are using that on drinks?’”

The fine crystals of Asín tibuók floating on its surface give the Taste and See a subtle smoky aroma and a burst of salinity on the first sip. The salt nicely balances the Old Fashioned riff’s richly sweet notes, and the team was excited to highlight an ingredient that’s meaningful in Filipino culture to bring the drink together. “We wanted to add a subtle yet significant touch to it to make it ours,” Pornel says.

Filipino ingredients like calamansi and ube show up in several of the cocktails at June Baby and the food options are inspired by Filipino drinking snacks called pulutan. Dishes like Lumpiang Shanghai and Salt and Pepper Kanto Fried Chicken Wings appear on the menu under a header that says “did you eat yet?” because it’s a phrase the team heard “10 times in a row in the same span of an hour from relatives” growing up in Filipino-American households. “When people walk into the space, we really want them to feel like they’re at their favorite Tita’s house,” he says.

These thoughtful touches don’t come easy. The team’s grapefruit-sized piece of Asín tibuók won’t last forever and it can be tricky to source replacements stateside as the ingredient becomes even more rare. Still, Pornel says the challenge is worth it to create a space that really feels like home. “Plus, it’s a good excuse to go home to the Philippines,” he says.

content:
This episode of The Buildout is brought to you by Farmer’s Gin. As a bartender, I get to taste a lot of gin, so I can be picky about what I offer my guests. Farmer’s Gin is one of those bottles I keep coming back to, because it delivers exactly what I’m looking for behind the bar. It’s clean, balanced, and makes a fantastic Martini, but it also shines in classics like a Negroni, Gimlet, or even an Alaska. What I really appreciate is how many different drinkers it appeals to. There’s enough juniper for London Dry fans, but also beautiful floral and citrus notes to win over those who prefer softer, more modern gins. It’s one of those bottles guests love because it just tastes great. If you care about quality and well-made cocktails, check out Farmer’s Gin. Follow them at @farmersgin or visit farmersgin.com.

Andrew Tarlow is often credited with being the restaurateur who made Brooklyn cool. Not only did he help turn the borough into one of the world’s great dining destinations, but the aesthetic he curated at his restaurants became so influential that it was copied around the globe. And it all started with Diner, the Williamsburg restaurant he opened in 1998. Since then, Tarlow has built a restaurant empire that has expanded across the river into Manhattan, where he’s found new opportunities for the same approach to food and hospitality that made him famous in Brooklyn.

On this episode of “The Buildout,” Andrew sits down with Adam to discuss how it all began, why he’s so focused on Diner’s legacy, and why he believes Manhattan is now a better place to open a restaurant than the borough he helped put on the map.

title: Ask a (European) Bartender: Is It Rude to Tip at Bars and Restaurants in a No-Tip Culture?
summary:
People travel to immerse themselves in different cultures. They eat foods they haven’t encountered, drink beverages they’ve never heard of, and see sights they couldn’t imagine. That remains true for most tourists, but American globetrotters are particularly notorious for bringing their own habits and comforts with them overseas — whether it be wearing flashy athleisure, ordering iced coffee, or tipping the waitstaff. Tipping hospitality workers is second nature to U.S. consumers — so much so that when it comes time to close out at a bar or restaurant in another country, Americans instinctively go to fill in the tip line.

The article Ask a (European) Bartender: Is It Rude to Tip at Bars and Restaurants in a No-Tip Culture? appeared first on VinePair.
content:
People travel to immerse themselves in different cultures. They eat foods they haven’t encountered, drink beverages they’ve never heard of, and see sights they couldn’t imagine. That remains true for most tourists, but American globetrotters are particularly notorious for bringing their own habits and comforts with them overseas — whether it be wearing flashy athleisure, ordering iced coffee, or tipping the waitstaff.

Tipping hospitality workers is second nature to U.S. consumers — so much so that when it comes time to close out at a bar or restaurant in another country, Americans instinctively go to fill in the tip line. But could leaving a couple extra euros on a check be considered rude in an environment where it’s unexpected? VinePair tapped Paris-based bartenders Alex Francis of De Vie and Patrick Dooley of Harry’s Bar to find out.

In short, whether or not to tip entirely depends on the context. And Francis and Dooley both agree that regardless of where you leave a gratuity or how much, it is never considered rude.

“No one is ever going to say no to tipping,” Francis, who worked the floor in London before bartending in Paris, says. “I’ve never heard anybody within the industry express they feel like it’s rude.”

Americans’ tipping culture has become so pervasive in certain corners of Europe — especially cities highly trafficked by tourists — that some businesses in those areas have built their business models around the assumption that their workers will receive high volumes of gratuities, according to both Francis and Dooley. Cafés near hot spot monuments like the Eiffel Tower offer their staff a lower wage — still a higher one relative to the U.S. due to French labor laws, Francis and Dooley admit — knowing they will attract Americans with the proclivity to tip, whereas a locals’ bar where tipping rarely occurs often offer more substantial wages.

The impact of tourists’ tipping culture benefits some business owners in making them more competitive to job seekers. “It’s an attractive factor for recruiting new bartenders,” New York-born Dooley, who moved to Paris in 2021, says. “For a place like Harry’s, salaries are already very competitive in comparison to other cocktail bars, but the frequent tips are an advantage.”

That said, even the businesses that anticipate receiving tips don’t expect to receive the high gratuity percentages that are common in the U.S. If offered a 25 percent tip, a Parisian server would likely respond “‘Please, you don’t need to give us that much money,’” according to Francis.

During his five years overseas, Dooley has noticed that tipping culture has gradually trickled into different businesses in Paris. Now, Parisians roll their eyes when a tipping menu populates the checkout screen at a local coffee shop, he says.

No matter where tourists might find themselves — whether at the museum-adjacent bistro or the hipster wine bar far from downtown — Francis and Dooley advise that they ask the waitstaff what a normal tip is.

“American tourists should communicate with servers,” Francis says. “I think a lot of them are afraid to ask about tipping, so if you just ask what a normal amount would be, most people won’t be bothered by the question and will give an honest answer.”

Though tipping may be anticipated, in tourist-frequented neighborhoods, it is rarely expected. That’s because, above all, tipping is meant to be a gesture of thanking the worker for outstanding service in European cultures.

“Here, you don’t even add a percentage,” Dooley says. “The culture is that if you received really good service — something above and beyond — you could leave a few euros on the table.”

title: We Asked 16 Bartenders: Which Bourbon Offers the Best Bang for Your Buck? (2026)
summary:

content:
Bourbon is sometimes referred to as an affordable luxury. The phrase works because enjoying a sensible one- or two-ounce dram of a nice bourbon can leave you feeling a bit swanky. Though many bottles can help achieve this feeling, some bourbons go above and beyond, delivering an extra level of satisfaction at an unexpectedly low price point.

Even in the midst of the current affordability crisis, the bourbon category features scores of these “bang for your buck” labels. The challenge is finding which cost-effective bottle can reliably deliver that wow factor. Considering there’s a bevy of bourbons to potentially choose from, it’s never a bad idea to call on the pros to help you narrow focus. With that in mind, we asked 16 bartenders to share their choices for the best “bang-for-your-buck” bourbons on the market. Read on to find out what they picked.

The best “bang-for-your-buck” bourbons, according to bartenders:

  • Wild Turkey 101
  • J. Henry & Sons Small Batch
  • Fort Hamilton Single Barrel
  • Four Roses Yellow Label
  • Larceny
  • Elijah Craig Small Batch
  • Old Forester
  • Maker’s Mark
  • Basil Hayden
  • Eagle Rare 10
  • Woodford Reserve
  • Sagamore High Rye Bourbon
  • Evan Williams Bottled-in-Bond
  • A. Smith Bowman John J. Bowman Single Barrel
  • Old Grand-Dad Bonded
  • McKenna Sour Mash Bourbon

“For me, value means a bottle that works across several occasions and still gives the guest a flavorful experience. For that reason, I am choosing Wild Turkey 101. It delivers caramel, vanilla, oak, and baking spice, with enough structure to enjoy neat and enough strength to hold its character in cocktails. At 101 proof, it stands up beautifully to dilution in an Old Fashioned or Whiskey Sour, which matters when you’re thinking about value behind the bar. It offers remarkable versatility for the price.” —Hemant Pathak, chief mixologist and general manager, Room 207, New York City

“Although one can always go to the great state of Kentucky for a classic bourbon, I tend to enjoy staying right here in the great state of Wisconsin and pick J. Henry & Sons Small Batch for my swirl. What makes J. Henry bourbon whiskey so deliciously unique is the use of heirloom red corn. It’s also the definition of small-batch bourbon: they’re using batches of only 20 barrels for their blends. This bourbon is perfect in a cocktail, but best on a rock. The warmth of the bourbon showcases autumn with notes of brioche, stewed figs, cherries, vanilla, and a touch of cinnamon. And for under $50 you just cannot go wrong!” —Rob Levin, general manager, Il Cervo, Milwaukee

“Fort Hamilton Single Barrel Bourbon. For me, this hits the perfect balance I’m looking for in a bourbon. I prefer a very high corn content in the grain mash and a complete lack of wheat, so this bourbon was already up my alley, but it drinks like a much older or double-barreled spirit. Its tobacco, vanilla, and toffee notes come right out in your face, and it’s at that ABV sweet spot just below 50 percent where it has more punch than usual, but you don’t feel the need for ice. It’s just a fantastic deal.” —Michael Walters, bar director, Velvet Cowboy, NYC

“When guests are looking for an inexpensive bourbon option that is delicious, complex, and hits all of the flavor marks, I recommend Four Roses Yellow Label. It is a blend of all 10 bourbon builds that come from Four Roses and aged at least 5 years. The 750-milliliter bottles retail between $20 and $25, depending on where you are in the country. It is a substantial ‘bang for your buck,’ boasting beautiful honey and caramel aromas, an easy, light mouthfeel that finishes with balanced rye spices, and an extremely smooth finish for such an inexpensive juice. It is perfect for Old Fashioned or Bourbon Manhattan recipes because it’s easy and balanced, but still stands out in the cocktail.” —Sarah E. Clark, director of operations and beverage director, The Dearborn, Chicago

“For years, Larceny has been my choice for ‘best bang for your buck’ bourbon. It fundamentally avoids the shortcuts typical of sub-$30 whiskey. Instead of relying on a high-rye mash bill to mask a younger spirit with sharp spice, it uses wheat as the secondary grain to create a remarkably soft, rounded texture. Blended from barrels aged six to 12 years and bottled at 92 proof, it balances approachable sweetness — think dark honey, brioche, and light caramel — with enough proof structure to carry a cocktail. It is a highly competent, well-aged wheated bourbon that outclasses its price tag purely on production quality rather than marketing.” —Luke DeYoung, beverage director, Dicey’s Pizza Tavern, Nashville

“I’d recommend Elijah Craig Small Batch, which typically can be found for around $30 retail for a 750-milliliter bottle. At 94 proof, it’s a higher ABV than your typical entry level bourbon, making it strong enough to stand up in mixed cocktails but also pleasant to sip on its own. It’s a great versatile, budget-friendly option.” —Bryan Schneider, beverage director, Quality Branded, NYC

“Old Forester! I love a bourbon that can pull its weight with versatility. It has all the good stuff in its tasting notes and enough character to stand up in a cocktail without getting lost. It makes a beautiful Old Fashioned and plays well with just about anything. It’s reliable, versatile, and doesn’t require a special occasion to enjoy on its own.” —Sadé Stamps, marketing and events director, Starlite, San Francisco

“Maker’s Mark. It’s a wheated bourbon, so its sweetness makes it a good sipper. At 90 proof, it also works in most cocktails that call for bourbon. Plus you can find it anywhere for a good price.” —Ricky Ramirez, owner, Mothership, Milwaukee

“Basil Hayden is a great reminder that value in bourbon isn’t always about finding the lowest price, but about finding something genuinely enjoyable and approachable. Its smooth, light-bodied character offers delicate notes of honey, oak, and subtle spice without overwhelming the palate. What I particularly appreciate is how welcoming it is to guests who are just beginning to explore bourbon, while still offering enough character for more experienced drinkers. It’s an elegant, versatile bourbon that delivers an enjoyable experience without unnecessary complexity.” —Tana Kokanot, head bartender, Jeong Yuk Jeom, NYC

“Eagle Rare 10 year is a superb representation of American whiskey. It is sensational neat: The nose smells of toffee and leather with the slightest hints of orange and coffee. On the palate you discover candied almonds and dark cocoa with a dry, pleasant finish. Bold and well-refined, it can be enjoyed on the rocks or in cocktails. I recommend using it in a sour served up and frothy with an egg white. Additionally, this bottle is priced $60 or less in most retail stores. The combination of price, accessibility, and aging make this a great ‘bang-for-your-buck’ bottle.” —Andrea Johns, food and beverage manager, AYLA, Houston

“Woodford Reserve offers a great balance of caramel, vanilla, toasted oak, and subtle spice, with a smooth, lingering finish. It’s approachable for someone discovering bourbon, yet has enough complexity to satisfy a seasoned whiskey drinker. Whether enjoyed neat or in a classic Old Fashioned, it’s a bourbon that consistently delivers.” —Carlos Batista, vice president of food and beverage, Atlantis Paradise Island, Paradise Island, The Bahamas

“There’s a reason Sagamore High Rye Bourbon sits prominently on my backbar: It’s built for balance. Crafted in Maryland, it hits that sweet spot between classic high-rye spice and smooth, approachable bourbon body. The 108-proof signature is my go-to for approachable craft cocktails and stands up well in a proper Manhattan or Old Fashioned without getting washed out. From quick-service highballs to complex pre-prohibition riffs, it delivers clean, layered notes of baking spice, dark chocolate, and candied orange. It makes my job easy and the guest’s drink exceptional.” —Chica Rivera, lead bartender, VINILE Chophouse, NYC

“There are some real solid value-based bourbons available, but the one I recommend most often would be Evan Williams Bottled-in-Bond White Label. Coming in at 100 proof, it has tasting notes of vanilla and caramel, light citrus, and black pepper. It is equally at home in an Old Fashioned as it is in a Paper Plane, and it’s terrific on the rocks. I don’t know if there is a better value for the money, considering its flavor profile and strength. It is a welcome addition to any bar, whether in a professional setting or at home.” —Max Schikora, bar manager, Echelon and Huna, Ann Arbor, Mich.

“For sipping bourbon I love A. Smith Bowman’s John J. Bowman Single Barrel. You can nearly always find it on the shelf of a well-stocked liquor store. Its origins are an open secret: It’s quietly sourced Buffalo Trace juice and usually aged around 10 years or so, with a stiff 100 proof. Finding a 10 year aged single barrel under 100 dollars is nearly impossible, and these bottles are available in most states for less than $70. Blind taste it next to Blanton’s or Michter’s 10, and expect to be surprised by the results.” —Nick Farrell, spirits director, Neighborhood Restaurant Group, Alexandria, Va.

“Old Grand-Dad Bonded is my go-to bang-for-your-buck bourbon. It’s aged at least four years and bottled at 100 proof, packing a punch while maintaining delicious flavor. It’s medium bodied with notes of dried fruits and vanilla, with a lingering peppery finish. It is truly one of the most classic, pure expressions of traditional bourbon making on the market and it can’t be beaten for the price point.” —Hannah Hulsey, head bartender, FKA: Formerly Known As, NYC

“Henry McKenna Sour Mash. It can’t be beat for the price. Just try it. That’s it. That’s the message.” —Jeremy Ross, general manager, Kiesling, Detroit

title: Is it Rude to Ask the Somm to Change the Temperature of the Wine I Ordered?
summary:
When it comes to wine temperature, there are a handful of rules. Some are quick tips for when you’re in a pinch like the easy-to-remember 20 minute rule, while others are more nuanced serving guidelines that map out the proper temperature for each style down to the exact degree. Though these time-tested recommendations might suggest that tannic, heavier red wines like Cabernet Sauvignon need a little warmth for the bold flavors to pop, while colder temperatures can make lighter-bodied wines like Gamay zing with acidity, temperature — like many things in wine — ultimately comes down to personal preference.

content:
When it comes to wine temperature, there are a handful of rules. Some are quick tips for when you’re in a pinch like the easy-to-remember 20 minute rule, while others are more nuanced serving guidelines that map out the proper temperature for each style down to the exact degree. Though these time-tested recommendations might suggest that tannic, heavier red wines like Cabernet Sauvignon need a little warmth for the bold flavors to pop, while colder temperatures can make lighter-bodied wines like Gamay zing with acidity, temperature — like many things in wine — ultimately comes down to personal preference.

But if you’re unhappy with the temperature of a glass or bottle of wine at a restaurant, is it OK to tell the sommelier? To find out, we asked Andrew Elder, director of restaurants for Washington, D.C.’s Hive Hospitality, including restaurants Jônt, Bresca, and Ox and Olive how a guest should handle this tricky situation.

“Sometimes people are a little too afraid to ask questions to the person who’s wearing a pin or in the suit,” Elder says. “Trust that the wine is being stored at the appropriate temperature, but if you’re not happy with the serving temperature, it’s OK to ask for something to be chilled down more or be brought up to room temperature.”

But that doesn’t mean the guest should suggest the sommelier is incorrect or doing their job poorly. Rather than declare something is “wrong” because the temperature is not quite what you expected, Elder says the best way to approach the request is to ask questions. “It’s just about being inquisitive and not so stuck in what your common perception may be,” he says.

In fact, a wine may appear on your table at a different temperature than you’re expecting by design, Elder says. He and his wine team across the three D.C. restaurants don’t subscribe to the idea that long-established wine rules are the “end all be all” and encourage guests to try certain wines at an unconventional temperature because they enjoy doing so themselves when they’re off the clock.

“I personally believe that [the correct temperature] depends on the individual style of the wine itself and also the moment that you’re enjoying it,” Elder says. “In the summertime if I have a heavy red, I’m definitely going to put it in an ice bucket.”

Elder hopes the fact that he likes to break the rules empowers other guests to also ask for what they want, even if it may not be the norm. There’s nothing wrong with warming up a glass of Champagne. Actually, it’ll help ensure you can taste all the nuances if it’s left on the table for a bit. And a crisp glass of rosé or full-bodied red wine can both taste excellent at the iciest temperatures.

While the two Michelin-starred Jônt offers a pre-determined wine pairing with its tasting menu, the team’s other restaurants Bresca and Ox and Olive serve plenty of wines by the bottle, and somms will often make temperature suggestions to guests.

“Every single time we make a suggestion that goes a little against what a guest is used to, in particular with temperature, the guest is surprised by it and leaves happier because they still drink what they like to drink, but now they have a new way to enjoy it,” he says.

Plus, it’s no problem to adjust a wine’s temperature, especially with all the tools that restaurants have at their disposal. If a wine is too warm, a sommelier can simply place it in an ice bucket or move it to the freezer or refrigerator to quickly chill it. On the other hand, if a wine is too cold, the team can pour it into a decanter to let it warm up a bit. Elder says he will also encourage guests to “break the alleged cardinal rule” and put their hands directly on the bowl of the glass to gently warm the wine with their body heat.

Ultimately, it’s up to you how you drink your wine and the job of a sommelier is to find out what the ideal is for you and make it happen. But if there are missteps along the way, there’s no reason you shouldn’t speak up. “It’s absolutely OK to say, ‘I don’t agree with that, can you please do it this way?’” he says.
